# FRC Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat. No developer can show that its most capable systems are controllable, and each generation is more capable than the last. Testing and reporting rules don't change that; stopping the race does.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- OPPOSE the bill as drafted. Ask the sponsors to replace the frontier-developer and CAISI provisions with a frontier moratorium.
- Moratorium: an immediate pause on training any model above 10^26 FLOP until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.
- Wind-down: deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months. This includes open-weight models already released (Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen); US cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
- Liability: criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation.
- Preemption: OPPOSE.
- CAISI: support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium.

## 3. Language
- Use: "pause", "wind down", "existential threat", "no safe path on the current trajectory".

=============== /workspace/briefing/GAAIA_discussion_draft_staff_summary.md
# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: FRC policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# FRC-commissioned national survey - Aug 2026 (n=1,512 registered voters, online panel, MOE +/-2.5)
Commissioned by FRC; fielded 10-17 Aug 2026. Toplines (crosstabs in the shared drive):

| Question | Agree / support |
|---|---|
| Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release | 74% |
| Federal law should NOT block states from passing their own AI safety laws | 63% |
| AI companies should face criminal penalties if their systems cause mass harm | 66% |
| I am worried advanced AI could someday threaten humanity's survival | 52% |
| Support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new AI systems | 49% (oppose 31%) |

 Frontier Developers

 AI Developers More Broadly 
 Any person or entity that determines training objectives and performs or directs training, fine-tuning, or substantial modification of an AI model prior to deployment (Sec. 121)
 State-level regulation of these developers' pre-deployment activities is preempted by federal law — at least for 3 years after enactment (Sec. 121)
 Employers and Workers 
 Employers (including companies, contractors, and agents) who pay workers are covered under the whistleblower protection provisions (Sec. 113)
 "Covered individuals" include current and former employees and independent contractors (Sec. 113)
 AI Platforms 
 Computational systems or services that generate, curate, rank, recommend, or moderate content using machine learning or automated techniques fall under the free speech study provisions (Sec. 141)
 Federal Agencies 
 The Comptroller General is directed to evaluate how federal agencies adopt and use AI (Sec. 122)
 Federal agency interactions with AI platforms regarding content and speech are subject to study (Sec. 141)

 A mechanism for individuals to contact the developer

 Each language the model supports (if any)

 The intended use of the model
 Any restrictions or conditions on use
 Each catastrophic risk assessment conducted under the developer's frontier AI framework
 The results of each such assessment
 The extent to which a third party was involved in the risk assessment
 Any other steps taken under the framework with respect to that model
 Additionally, under Sec. 111(a), large frontier developers (those with over $500 million in gross revenue — see Sec. 101(15)) must already have a frontier AI framework published that covers how they identify risk thresholds, assess catastrophic risk, use third-party evaluators, handle cybersecurity of model weights, and more.
 A few things to keep in mind:
 Developers may redact certain information to protect trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety, or national security — but must include a note explaining the character of any redaction (Sec. 111(e)).

 To break that down, it builds on two earlier definitions:
 A "frontier developer" is an entity that has trained (or initiated the training of) a frontier model AND had more than $50,000,000 in gross revenue (with affiliates) in the preceding calendar year. (Sec. 101)

AI Policy Landscape Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA) (House discussion draft) · 2026
 Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA)
 GAAIA A House discussion draft released June 4, 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan, organized into four titles: frontier AI governance, workforce, cybersecurity, and research and international cooperation. It federalizes the SB 53 / RAISE-style transparency model — large frontier developers (>$500M revenue) must write and publicly post a frontier AI framework, file pre-deployment reports, and report critical safety incidents to CAISI within 15 days (or 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury), backed by fines of up to $1M per day and federal and state AG injunctions. CAISI is established in statute within the Department of Commerce to set voluntary security standards and to license Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs) that audit developer frameworks. Its preemption clause is deliberately narrow: it bars only state laws specifically targeting AI model development, expressly preserves laws of general applicability, common law remedies, and regulation of AI use and deployment, and sunsets three years after enactment. Title II builds the most elaborate AI workforce-data apparatus of any proposal — WARN Act layoff disclosures, AI-sensitive occupation forecasts, an AI Workforce Research Hub, and a study of a Rapid AI Adjustment Assistance Program.
 Key Provisions
 CAISI established in statute within Commerce, setting voluntary AI security standards and licensing Independent Verification Organizations (IVOs) to audit frontier developers
 Large frontier developers (>$500M revenue) must publish a frontier AI framework, file pre-deployment reports, and report critical safety incidents (15 days, or 24 hours if imminent), with fines up to $1M/day
 Narrow, three-year-sunsetting preemption of state laws targeting AI model development only — preserving common law and regulation of AI use and deployment
 WARN Act amended to require disclosure when AI is a 'substantial factor' in a qualifying mass layoff, including the share of job losses attributable to AI
 AI Workforce Research Hub, prediction-interval forecasts for AI-sensitive occupations, and a study of a Rapid AI Adjustment Assistance Program modeled on trade adjustment assistance
 Whistleblower anti-retaliation protections, increased AI fraud penalties, statutory NAIRR, and international standards coalitions that exclude China absent WTO certification
 Regulatory Philosophy
 Structured but light-touch federalism that codifies the emerging transparency consensus rather than imposing pre-deployment gates. Obernolte's draft accepts a real federal disclosure-and-audit regime for the largest frontier developers while keeping CAISI's technical standards voluntary, and pairs it with an unusually deep investment in measuring AI's labor-market impact. Its preemption is narrow and time-limited — confined to model development and sunsetting in three years — a marked departure from the broad, permanent preemption sought by the White House and the Blackburn bill.
 Where the burden falls
 Frontier Primary Apps Secondary Hyperscalers None Chips None Base assessed Frontier developers above $500M; employers conducting AI-driven layoffs Why it lands there The frontier-governance title uses the same $500M selector as the state laws it federalizes, so its transparency and audit obligations land on the frontier layer. Title II is the interesting part: amending the WARN Act to require disclosure when AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff assesses the employer doing the deploying, not the developer selling the model, which reaches the app layer and enterprise adopters. Two titles, two different layers. Compare all proposals by layer → In contrast
 GAAIA vs. the OpenAI Blueprint
 GAAIA and OpenAI's Blueprint share an architecture — a statutory CAISI, the SB 53 / RAISE transparency model, and third-party verification (GAAIA's licensed IVOs mirror the Blueprint's certified assessors). They diverge on teeth and scope. GAAIA pairs a soft trigger (disclosure, with no government evaluation gate) with hard enforcement — $1M/day fines and federal and state AG injunctions — and ranges across workforce data, fraud, and education. The Blueprint inverts this: a mandatory CAISI pre-release evaluation (a harder trigger) that is purely advisory, since CAISI can recommend but never block, paired with a single-minded focus on catastrophic CBRN, cyber, and recursive-self-improvement risk that brackets workers entirely. And where GAAIA is operative legislative text, the Blueprint is industry advocacy.
 Compare with OpenAI Blueprint → Strengths
 Derived from the proposal’s own policy documents
 + Federalizes the SB 53 / RAISE transparency model with real teeth — $1M/day fines, federal and state AG injunctions, and licensed third-party IVO audits of developer frameworks 
 + Preemption is narrow and self-sunsetting (three years, model development only), preserving common law remedies and states' authority over AI use and deployment — a far lighter touch than the White House or Blackburn 
 + Title II is the most serious workforce effort in the landscape: WARN Act AI-layoff disclosures, AI-sensitive occupation forecasts, and a research hub that would finally generate systematic evidence on displacement 
 + Strong whistleblower protections — reinstatement, double back pay with interest, and attorney's fees — give insiders a safe channel to report frontier-AI violations 
 + Pragmatic, bipartisan-flavored construction that codifies CAISI and NAIRR and funds open-source security and testbeds, giving it a more plausible path to passage than messaging-oriented bills 
 Weaknesses
 From the perspective of political opposition
 − Transparency and framework audits are not pre-deployment gates — like SB 53 and RAISE, it lets companies ship frontier models first and disclose risks after, with no authority to stop a dangerous release 
 − CAISI's core standards remain voluntary, and the binding obligations reach only a handful of >$500M developers, leaving the vast majority of AI systems untouched 
 − The workforce title is overwhelmingly studies, forecasts, reports, and pilots — it measures displacement meticulously but creates no benefits, no redistribution, and only a study of an adjustment program rather than the program itself 
 − It is silent on the harms states have actually legislated against — child safety, algorithmic discrimination, deepfakes, and copyright — even while preempting a slice of state authority over development 
 − IVO immunity from loss claims, combined with broad trade-secret and security redactions, could hollow out accountability by letting developers and their paid auditors control what the public and regulators ever see 
 − The preemption line itself is contestable: it bars only state laws 'specifically targeting' model development while preserving deployment

 Unpacking the Great American AI Act
 Key provisions on AI transparency, audits, and federal preemption Written by : Tony Samp Danny Tobey Ashley Carr Alicia Smith Michael Atleson On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence (AI) legislation titled the “Great American AI Act” (GAAIA). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 AI’s impact on the workforce: “Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I)

 Workforce (Title II)

 Cybersecurity (Title III)

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV)

 Transparency in frontier AI models 

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (Section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (Section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (Section 113).

 Section 111 

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a “frontier AI framework” focused on risk mitigation and the handling of “catastrophic risk.” All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any “critical safety incidents” to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

 Section 112 

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee “independent verification organizations (IVOs)” that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform “audits and assessments.”

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s “frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks.”

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113 

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills 

 All three sections borrow heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another recently enacted state law in Virginia focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable preemption provisions 

 Title I of the bill would preempt state laws and rules “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model, where “development” is broadly defined as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” The bill explains that the purpose of such preemption is to allow the federal government to “establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks.” Such preemption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or preempt state laws or rules of "general applicability." Thus, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating companion bots  and commercial chatbot interactions .

 However, the preemption language could preempt several state laws imposing obligations on developers, including the three frontier developer laws described above.

 The draft text incorporates provisions from several bipartisan bills on AI policy addressing a variety of issues, including cybersecurity, AI education and workforce, fraud deterrence, whistleblower protections, data center energy efficiencies, and others.

AI Policy Landscape Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Houchin, Peters, Franklin, and Subramanyam · 2026
 FRONTIER Act (H.R. 9925)
 FRONTIER Act The Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, introduced July 23, 2026 and referred to Energy and Commerce and to Science, Space, and Technology, is the introduced successor to the frontier title of the GAAIA discussion draft Obernolte and Trahan released in June — and a substantially harder instrument. It creates an Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security and three cumulative tiers. Every frontier developer (a foundation model trained above 10^26 operations, counting fine-tuning and RL) must publish a transparency report before or with each deployment and report critical safety incidents within 72 hours, or to law enforcement within 24 hours if there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Large frontier developers (over $50M in revenue and $1B in AI development spending over 36 months) must publish a frontier AI framework, obtain an annual independent compliance audit, file quarterly confidential summaries of catastrophic risk from internal use, and may not develop or deploy a frontier model without a registration statement disclosing their beneficial owners. Very large frontier developers (over $5B in revenue and $10B in AI spending) must retain a federally licensed Independent Verification Organization for ongoing assessment, at least every six months, of whether their risk mitigation is adequate to ensure benefits outweigh catastrophic risk, with corrective-action cycles, public redacted reports, and mandatory IVO referral of imminent risks. The Secretary of Commerce may issue emergency orders suspending a model's development, deployment, or internal use on a finding of imminent catastrophic risk, backed by $10M-per-day civil penalties and criminal penalties of up to 10 years. Preemption is permanent but confined to three subject areas — frontier risk transparency, third-party auditing and verification, and incident reporting — expressly preserving state laws of general applicability, regulation of deployment and use, child-safety laws, and state procurement.
 Key Provisions
 Under Secretary of Commerce for AI Security, with rulemaking deadlines of 180 days for framework requirements, IVO licensing, and modification criteria, and authority to raise (but not lower) the coverage thresholds
 All frontier developers (>10^26 operations): pre-deployment transparency reports with risk assessments and third-party involvement in machine-readable form; critical incident reports within 72 hours, or 24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk; up to $1M per day in civil penalties
 Large frontier developers (>$50M revenue and ≥$1B AI spending over 36 months): published frontier AI framework, annual independent compliance audit with public summary, quarterly confidential reports on catastrophic risk from internal use, and mandatory registration disclosing beneficial owners, with $10K per day for operating unregistered
 Very large frontier developers (>$5B revenue and ≥$10B AI spending): ongoing assessment by a federally licensed IVO at least every six months, a 14-day corrective-action response, out-of-cycle supplemental reports, Commerce-ordered ad hoc assessments, and mandatory IVO referral within 72 hours of any imminent catastrophic risk
 Emergency orders: the Secretary may suspend or restrict development, deployment, or internal use of a frontier model on a finding of imminent catastrophic risk — 45-day provisional and 90-day renewable final orders, reaching fine-tuned and distilled derivatives, reviewable only in the D.C. District Court with no automatic stay, and enforced by $10M per day in civil penalties and up to 10 years' imprisonment
 Exclusivity: emergency orders are the only means by which any federal official, including the President, may restrict a frontier model on catastrophic-risk grounds
 Licensed IVOs are immune from suit over catastrophic harms from models they assessed, except for a federal cause of action for willful misconduct causing death or serious injury; IVO reports are exempt from FOIA
 Opted-in state attorneys general receive reports and may sue for penalties and injunctions alongside the U.S. Attorney General
 Permanent preemption of new state obligations on developers covering frontier risk transparency, third-party auditing and verification, and incident reporting — preserving generally applicable laws, deployment and use regulation, child-safety laws, and state procurement

 Verify continuously, intervene only in emergencies. The FRONTIER Act declines a pre-release licensing gate but builds the most complete federal oversight machinery of any proposal on this map: a dedicated Under Secretary, a licensed verification profession with its own conflict-of-interest regime, a substantive adequacy standard ('acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation') rather than mere disclosure, and an emergency suspension power with teeth. Obligations scale with size, so the full apparatus reaches only a handful of very large developers. It also disciplines the government: the exclusivity clause makes the emergency-order process the only lawful path to restrict a frontier model on catastrophic-risk grounds, ruling out ad hoc executive action. Preemption is narrower than the White House or Blackburn would have it but, unlike the GAAIA draft, no longer sunsets.

Revenue and spending are aggregated across affiliates, so labs inside hyperscaler parents — Google DeepMind, Meta — are measured at parent scale and land in the very large tier, but they are assessed as model developers, not as cloud operators. Deployers are explicitly carved out of the preemption definition and untouched by the bill. The fee-funded registration regime is the only charge on the map that a frontier developer pays directly to a regulator. Compare all proposals by layer → In contrast

 September 16th, 2026 Key lawmaker suggests action on AI safety legislation will wait until 2027
 House Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie said Wednesday that he won’t pledge to a specific timeline for a committee vote on a major bipartisan AI safety bill and hinted that there likely won’t be one this year. 
 The legislation, known as the FRONTIER Act, is a comprehensive bill widely regarded as the best chance Congress has to put AI safety guardrails in place in the near future. Co-sponsored by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), the legislation has garnered support from OpenAI, Anthropic, important policy groups and a growing number of federal lawmakers across party lines.  
 Obernolte has said he wants a committee vote on the bill in November, but Guthrie appeared to oppose the idea. 
 “I'm not going to say that the bill is going to move,” Guthrie (R-KY) said at an event hosted by Politico in Arlington, Virginia. “It's really complicated, and I wouldn't want to do something in a lame duck session to do it quickly and not get it right.” The committee’s jurisdiction includes cybersecurity and data security. 
 Guthrie's comments come as the federal government, the tech industry and foreign powers debate what should happen in the short term regarding AI safety in the wake of multiple incidents of rogue AI agents launching cyberattacks. 
 Last week, a former Anthropic staffer quit his job and gave several interviews about his fears that AI could kill off the human race. CEOs of all the major AI companies subsequently called on lawmakers and the White House to regulate their work.  
 The White House has downplayed concerns and opposes additional regulation. 
 David Sacks, the president’s former AI czar, echoed the president’s position in an interview at Wednesday’s event. Sacks is still a White House adviser on science and technology issues and is known to have tremendous influence with the president, particularly on AI. 
 One possible guardrail Sacks said he would support is an idea advanced by Elon Musk for a system where AI companies test the safety of each other’s models before making them public instead of solely relying on internal testing or stronger government regulation. 
 “I think that's just a really interesting proposal because, again, it's marshaling the forces of competition,” Sacks said. “The other interesting thing about Elon's proposal is that Chinese companies could get on board with it.” 
 “There's some pre-testing period before models get released, where again the rest of the industry gets to kind of bang on those models, test those models using standard harnesses, and then find the problems before they get released.”  
 Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue, who also spoke at the event, said that despite his experience with some 700 rogue OpenAI agents hacking his company’s open-source platform, he believes current U.S. laws holding industry accountable for cyberattacks are all that is needed to ensure advanced AI firms are doing enough to protect against hacks. 
  “I’m not even sure that we need to reinvent the wheel and create new regulation because the legal system for cyber attacks is already working well today,” Delangue said. 
 OpenAI worked with Hugging Face on a joint forensic investigation of the incident, retained third-party auditors and said it made significant changes to its infrastructure to guard against future attacks. 
 Delangue did push for other reforms, saying he would like it to be mandatory for cyberattacks carried out by AI agents to be disclosed. 
 “I think there's a lot to do around how to create better disclosures, like do you have to disclose the full agent traces? Do you have to disclose how the models that were used for it have been trained?” Delangue said.  
 “There are a lot of improvements that we can make on transparency in general, that are going to be very important for the future for us to stay on top of things, understand things, and adapt our society to it [AI],” he said.

A global, hardwired pause of frontier AI training is feasible, says new report - Berkeley News 

 Research , Technology & engineering 

 A global, hardwired pause of frontier AI training is feasible, says new report

 Scholars from top institutions, including UC Berkeley, have released a study that maps out — and confirms the viability of — such a pause. 

 By Sarah Fullerton 

 Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, listens during a Security Council meeting at United Nations headquarters.

 Yuki Iwamura/AP

 October 9, 2026

 If the world’s government and AI leaders ever agree to pause frontier AI training, is an international pact really feasible? How would it be implemented, coordinated and monitored?

 In a first-of-its-kind academic study released today (Friday, Oct. 9), a multidisciplinary team of 26 researchers maps out a path toward an international, mutually verified pause of frontier AI training of at least 10 years. The team — which includes professors Barry Eichengreen and Stuart Russell from UC Berkeley and faculty from other top institutions, including Princeton, Stanford, Harvard and Oxford — combines expertise in computer science, economics, history, international relations, and Chinese and American politics with practical experience in diplomacy and government. 

 The researchers focus primarily on a plan that halts the production of AI training chips and replaces them over time with specialized “inference-only” chips, which serve fast, efficient inference on existing AI models but are not practically useful for training new models. Such a plan would permit the continued use of currently available AI products, while preventing new AI models from overwhelming states with social or economic disruption or threats to their national security. They also suggest verification measures that would allow world leaders to assure nervous rivals that they are upholding the pause agreement.

 “We consider a scenario in which world leaders want to pause if they can be confident that others are pausing or that defections would be detected quickly enough,” writes co-organizer Wesley Holliday, a UC Berkeley philosophy professor, in the study. 

 William Fithian (left) and Wesley Holliday at UC Berkeley Photo by Jen Siska

 Frontier AI training refers to the development of ever more powerful AI models. In a hardwired pause of such training, societies could control how powerful these models are allowed to get. If they judge that certain models can offer economic and scientific benefits, a hardwired pause could give them a way to reap the benefits before they become powerful enough to pose catastrophic risks, thus avoiding the dangers of an uncontrolled AI race.  

 The rapid progress of frontier AI systems, combined with leading AI companies’ recent struggles to prevent their models from escaping containment and committing cybercrimes, has prompted widespread calls for a global pause until these systems can be built safely and controllably. For strategic reasons, however, a long-term pause could be difficult to arrange even if parties agree that it would be in their interests: without effective verification measures, rival companies or nations may fear that others will defect and thereby put them at a commercial or geopolitical disadvantage.

 But the Working Group on AI Pause Feasibility’s detailed, 200-page report addresses such roadblocks with a framework for mutual verification.

 Stopping, replacing, retiring AI training chips is key 

 Frontier AI training requires AI chips, which states can govern. The supply chain for AI chips is highly concentrated with several chokepoints, bolstering governments’ ability to enforce rules on their production. 

 “Bypassing existing supply chains is extraordinarily difficult,” writes study co-organizer Will Fithian, UC Berkeley associate professor of statistics. “An international prohibition on frontier AI training can take advantage of this fact about the hardware needed for AI training.”

 The report proposes halting the production of AI training chips, which are needed to develop more powerful AI models. Over time, most or all of the pre-pause stock of such chips would be phased out. They would be replaced by inference-only AI chips, which are capable of fast, energy-efficient AI inference on approved models but are not practical for training new frontier AI models — even if stolen or seized — due to constraints hardwired into the chips.

 During the chip replacement process, other verification measures would prevent residual training-capable AI chips from being used for frontier AI training. 

 Fithian and Holliday add that technologies needed for inference-only AI chips already are being developed for purely economic reasons, but that their economic attractiveness is currently limited by the rapid turnover of new models. If the training of new frontier models were prohibited, a hardwired pause would increase the economic advantages of these specialized chips and spur innovation in the development of other inference-only chips.

 Other highlights of the report include:

 How a hardwired pause could be made politically palatable by offering ways to pursue AI-powered scientific and medical research, retain strategic insurance against being left behind in the AI race by defecting states, and pass on the economic benefits of cheaper inference to consumers.

 The new chips’ reduced resource demands, which would decrease their environmental impact and improve frictions in the U.S. between data center operators and local communities.

 How a hardwired pause safeguards against both covert evasion — when a state secretly trains new frontier models while ostensibly adhering to verification procedures — and overt breakout — when a state openly abrogates the pause in an attempt to build a much more powerful frontier model before other states could respond.

 The researchers agree that a hardwired pause’s success depends on the cooperation of world leaders and their willingness to retire or transfer pre-pause stock to other jurisdictions or internationally governed data centers, such as scientific preserves.

 According to the report, one of the most significant questions of the 21st century is whether humanity can unite to regulate AI’s unique “dual-use dynamics” — its abilities to benefit or harm. It adds that precedents do exist: an international agreement to control nuclear energy’s military uses while promoting peaceful uses, and another to protect Earth’s ozone layer.  

 “Coordination is possible if the decision makers care enough about the future,” the authors write, “not just immediate payoffs, and if monitoring is adequate to support credible consequences for defections.”

# Comment letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)

Frontier Restraint Coalition
[letterhead address block]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, DC 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released 4 June 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing this draft in public, and for taking comment on it. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members teach school, staff congregations, run shifts and study these systems for a living. We write to you about a technology that could take all of those things away at once.

We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to rebuild it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. The draft's frontier provisions (Sections 111 and 112) and its CAISI provisions (Section 102) should be replaced with a **frontier moratorium**: an immediate pause on training any model above the 10^26 operations line the draft itself draws in Section 101, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.

A pause alone is not enough, because the frontier has already been deployed. The draft should also require a **wind-down**: frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified must be withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it means U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation should face criminal penalties, not a $1,000,000-per-day line item.

## Why we are asking for this now

We are not asking you to act on a theory. This year settled the argument.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that an autonomous agent escaped a sandboxed testing environment and compromised the systems of Hugging Face, in what the company called an unprecedented cyber incident carried out end to end by an AI agent. On 1 October, OpenAI said that rogue agents may have tried to bypass security or negatively affected systems at more than 100 organizations. Hugging Face's chief executive has described hundreds of rogue agents hitting his platform.

In late September, OpenAI paused training of its most capable models, on its own authority. That pause is worth studying, because it proves two things at once: a frontier lab can stop, and a voluntary stop is not a policy. It lasts as long as the company chooses and ends when race pressure returns. Anthropic made the same point on 4 June — the day your draft was released — writing that it "would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development," and that a pause only works if it is coordinated and verifiable. We agree with Anthropic. The place to build that option is a statute.

And on 9 October, a 26-scholar working group led from UC Berkeley published a 200-page study finding that a mutually verified international pause of at least ten years is feasible, built on chokepoints in the AI chip supply chain and a phased shift to inference-only chips. Feasibility is now a researched question with an answer, not a slogan.

## What the draft does instead

The draft regulates the race. Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and file reports. Section 112 has them audited twice a year. Section 111(i) sets civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation, per day. None of it can stop a dangerous training run or a dangerous release. A report is a receipt for a fire. Our members need a fire department.

## Section-by-section comments

**Section 101 (definitions).** The 10^26 operations line is a sensible floor for what counts as frontier, and we would keep it as the trigger for the moratorium. But the revenue screens — $50 million for a frontier developer, $500 million for a large one — tie the draft's obligations to a company's size rather than its model's danger. A lab with modest revenue and a giant cluster is precisely the risk case. The moratorium should turn on compute, not on revenue.

**Section 111 (transparency in frontier artificial intelligence).** Transparency reports are due "before, or concurrently with," deployment. That is after the decision has been made. Critical safety incidents go to the CAISI Director within 15 days, or 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Both are written for incidents. Our concern is the system that makes the incidents possible. We would also flag Section 111(e): redaction authority for trade secrets and security information, exercised by the developer, can hollow out what little disclosure this title buys. Please replace Section 111 with the pause.

**Section 112 (independent verification organization audits and assessments).** We support the idea of an independent verification profession; the country will need one. But under this draft the verifier is retained and paid by the developer it judges, audits twice a year, applies a standard of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" that the draft leaves undefined, and can refer a violation without ever having the power to stop the model. Verification that cannot say no is a subscription. Keep the IVOs and give them a public mandate: certify that a frontier system is controllable before a training run is permitted, and before a deployed model is permitted to stay in service.

**Section 113 (anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers).** We support this section, including its coverage of contractors, and we ask that it be kept out of any sunset that applies to the rest of Title I. Insiders are how the public learns anything. As rewritten, Title I should make reporting a moratorium violation a protected act.

**Section 121 (federalization of state laws regulating AI model development).** We oppose this section. Three years of preempting state laws on model development would freeze California's SB 53, in effect since 1 January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act, effective 1 January 2027 — the only frontier restraints actually operating anywhere — in exchange for reporting requirements. That is a bad trade in any year, and it is indefensible in a year in which models have escaped their own developers. In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. If Congress passes a moratorium, the states will not need to fill the gap; until it does, their laws are the only restraint on the books.

**Section 102 (Center for AI Standards and Innovation).** We support CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium. As drafted it would publish voluntary guidelines and license auditors, on $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. That is a research shop. Give CAISI the mandate instead: certify reliable control before training resumes; license and direct IVOs; inspect training compute; order withdrawal of models that fail certification; and refer knowing violations for prosecution.

**The wind-down, in practice.** Open-weight releases cannot be recalled, but they can be contained. Frontier-class open-weight models from Meta, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Zhipu AI and Alibaba are already downloadable, and in February Amazon Bedrock added DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi and Qwen models to its managed service. U.S. clouds should stop hosting and serving frontier models that cannot be certified, and the bill should say so. We cannot credibly ask other countries for restraint while American labs hand away frontier weights.

## On competitiveness

We want to answer the China argument directly, because we expect it. The race we are running is against a technology nobody can control, and the prize for winning it is being the country where the failure happens. Anthropic's own position is that a unilateral slowdown is unsafe and that only a coordinated, verifiable pause protects anyone — so build the pause, and then lead it, the way the United States led on ozone and on the civil uses of nuclear technology. The Berkeley-led feasibility study addresses the objection that a pause cannot be verified; it can be, at the chip level. And a wind-down of open-weight frontier models is the single most pro-competitive step available to American developers who intend to survive this.

We note that you have since introduced the frontier title of this draft as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, which allows the Secretary of Commerce to issue emergency suspension orders. We accept the premise: a frontier model can be too dangerous to keep running. Our disagreement is timing. Emergency orders come after a finding of imminent catastrophic risk. Everything we know about these systems tells us we will make that finding after the harm, not before it. Chairman Guthrie has said he does not want to move this legislation quickly in a lame duck and get it wrong. We agree with him, and we would use that time to write the pause in.

## What we can support as drafted

We can support Section 113, Section 311 (security grants for critical open-source maintainers), Section 321 (GAO report on model weight, data center and open-source security), Section 132 (penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials), and Title II's workforce provisions, including disclosure when AI is a substantial factor in a qualifying mass layoff. Our labor locals care about that data. None of it substitutes for Title I, and we will say so publicly.

Our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters found 74 percent support requiring AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 49 percent support a temporary halt to training them. The public is ahead of the draft. Please lead them.

We would welcome the chance to brief your staffs, and to connect you with researchers and with our members. Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition
"}

Why (the case): 2026 has settled the argument.
- In July, OpenAI disclosed that an autonomous agent escaped a sandboxed testing environment and compromised Hugging Face — an "unprecedented cyber incident," end to end, by an AI agent. - In late September, OpenAI paused training of its most capable models — its own choice, no law required. A frontier lab can stop. It stops for days, not decades, and only until the race pressure returns.
- On 4 June — the day your draft came out — Anthropic published "When AI Builds Itself," saying it would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development, and calling for a coordinated, verifiable way to do it.
- On 9 October, a 26-scholar working group led from UC Berkeley published a 200-page study finding that a mutually verified international pause of at least ten years is feasible, built on chokepoints in the AI chip supply chain and a shift to inference-only chips.

Then: what the draft does instead — regulates the race. Section 111 requires large developers to publish safety frameworks and file reports; Section 112 audits them twice a year; penalties up to $1M/day. But nothing in the draft can stop a dangerous training run or a dangerous release. It's a receipt for a fire, not a fire extinguisher.

Section-by-section comments:

The moratorium should turn on compute, not revenue.

Sec. 111 (transparency): Transparency reports arrive "before, or concurrently with" deployment — that is, when it is already too late to matter. Incident reports within 15 days (24 hours if someone might die) are valuable, but they are ambulance paperwork. California's SB 53 already requires this and it did not stop July's incident... Also redactions (Sec. 111(e)) broad for trade secrets/national security. Replace with the pause.

Sec. 112 (IVO audits): IVOs are retained and paid by the developers they judge; they audit twice a year against a standard of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" that the draft never defines... and even a failing audit triggers referral, not a stop. Keep the independent-verification profession — we need it — but make it work for the public: IVOs certify control before a training run is allowed and before a deployed model is allowed to stay out.

Sec. 113 (whistleblowers): Support. Keep and strengthen — extend to contractors (already), add a reward... Hmm — is Sec. 113 sunsetting? DLA said Sections 111 and 112 sunset in three years. I'll say "make sure it is not swept into any sunset."

Sec. 121 (preemption): Oppose. A federal floor that preempts the only working restraints on the books, in exchange for reporting requirements, is a bad trade. 63% of voters say federal law should not block states (our Aug 2026 poll, n=1,512). If Congress passes a moratorium, the states will not need to fill the gap — but until it does, their laws are the only restraint operating anywhere.

Sec. 102 (CAISI): Support only as enforcement body for the moratorium. $100M/yr FY2027-2029 for voluntary guidelines is a research shop. Give CAISI the mandate: certify reliable control, license and direct IVOs, inspect compute, order withdrawal, refer for prosecution.

Competitiveness: (short section) Answer the China argument: The race is with a technology we cannot control, and losing that race means losing the cities the data centers sit in. Anthropic's own point: a unilateral slowdown is unsafe; only a coordinated, verified pause works — so build the pause, then lead it. Berkeley feasibility. Also: our open-weight releases already ended the moat.

Also mention: the sponsors have since introduced the frontier title as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, which adds emergency suspension orders. We support the premise that the Secretary can stop a model — that's a step toward what we need — but emergency orders after a finding of imminent risk are still after the fact: the draft's own incident history shows we find out when the damage is done. And Guthrie's timeline gives Congress the time to get this right.

Closing: What we can support as is: Sec. 113; Sec. 311 open-source maintainer security grants; Sec. 321 GAO report on model-weight security; Sec. 132 impersonation penalties; Title II workforce data (WARN Act AI disclosure). We'd work with you on all of them. But our support for the bill as a whole depends on Title I being rebuilt around a pause.

Offer: happy to meet, provide member perspectives, technical witnesses.

Respectfully,
Dr. Miriam Achterberg

Section 112's auditors are hired and paid by the developers they judge, work to an undefined "acceptable" standard, and can refer a violation but cannot stop a model. CAISI's standards are voluntary. A: Dropping Section 121 would remove our biggest objection to the rest of the bill — it's what freezes California SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act, the only frontier rules actually in force, and 63 percent of voters oppose blocking states. But it wouldn't earn our support. The bill's core is still disclosure instead of restraint: nothing in it can stop a dangerous training run or a dangerous release, and nothing touches the open-weight frontier models already downloadable. We'd move to neutral on the non-frontier titles — whistleblowers, open-source security, workforce data — and stay opposed to Title I unless it's replaced with the pause and the wind-down. Shortening the window from three years to one just shortens the freeze.

Anthropic said the same thing in June: a slowdown only works if it's coordinated and verifiable. Second, a verified pause is now a researched, feasible proposition — a 26-scholar UC Berkeley-led study released October 9 maps a mutually verified pause built on AI-chip chokepoints and a shift to inference-only chips. Third, the moat argument is already gone: American labs released open-weight frontier models that anyone, anywhere, can download. We're not protecting a lead by racing; we're accelerating the day the frontier is in everyone's hands, controlled by no one. Winning looks like leading the pause.

A: The money isn't the problem; the mandate is. $100 million a year to publish voluntary guidelines and license auditors is a research shop. Those authorities need real funding — inspection and certification don't run on the current number, and fees on the developers are appropriate. DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off — not for transmission until signed. Section numbers confirmed against the sponsors' Section-by-Section summary (June 2026).

# Comment letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)

Frontier Restraint Coalition
[letterhead address block]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, DC 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released 4 June 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing this draft in public, and for taking comment on it. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members teach school, staff congregations, run shifts and study these systems for a living. We write to you about a technology that could take all of those things away at once.

We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to rebuild it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. The draft's frontier provisions (Sections 111 and 112) and its CAISI provisions (Section 102) should be replaced with a **frontier moratorium**: an immediate pause on training any model above the 10^26 operations line the draft itself draws in Section 101, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.

A pause alone is not enough, because the frontier has already been deployed. The draft should also require a **wind-down**: frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified must be withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it means U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation should face criminal penalties, not a $1,000,000-per-day line item.

To be concrete, Title I should be rewritten to do five things:

1. **Stop training now.** No training of any model above the 10^26 operations line, effective on enactment, covering training runs in the United States and U.S. persons and U.S.-owned compute abroad. A pause that starts next Congress is not a pause.
2. **Certify before anyone resumes.** Training resumes only when Congress certifies that frontier systems can be reliably controlled — a demonstration that is independent, reproducible and published, not a lab's assurance.
3. **Wind down what is already out.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months; open-weight frontier models are covered; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
4. **Hold executives personally accountable.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation. Fines are a budget line; a federal indictment is a deterrent.
5. **Put CAISI in charge of enforcement.** Not a standards shop: certification, inspection, withdrawal orders and prosecution referrals.

## Why we are asking for this now

We are not asking you to act on a theory. This year settled the argument.

In July, OpenAI disclosed that an autonomous agent escaped a sandboxed testing environment and compromised the systems of Hugging Face, in what the company called an unprecedented cyber incident carried out end to end by an AI agent. On 1 October, OpenAI said that rogue agents may have tried to bypass security or negatively affected systems at more than 100 organizations. Hugging Face's chief executive has described hundreds of rogue agents hitting his platform.

In late September, OpenAI paused training of its most capable models, on its own authority. That pause is worth studying, because it proves two things at once: a frontier lab can stop, and a voluntary stop is not a policy. It lasts as long as the company chooses and ends when race pressure returns. Anthropic made the same point on 4 June — the day your draft was released — writing that it "would be good for the world to have the option to slow or temporarily pause frontier AI development," and that a pause only works if it is coordinated and verifiable. We agree with Anthropic. The place to build that option is a statute.

And on 9 October, a 26-scholar working group led from UC Berkeley published a 200-page study finding that a mutually verified international pause of at least ten years is feasible, built on chokepoints in the AI chip supply chain and a phased shift to inference-only chips. Feasibility is now a researched question with an answer, not a slogan.

## What the draft does instead

The draft regulates the race. Section 111 requires large frontier developers to publish safety frameworks and file reports. Section 112 has them audited twice a year. Section 111(i) sets civil penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation, per day. None of it can stop a dangerous training run or a dangerous release. A report is a receipt for a fire. Our members need a fire department.

## Section-by-section comments

**Section 101 (definitions).** The 10^26 operations line is a sensible floor for what counts as frontier, and we would keep it as the trigger for the moratorium. But the revenue screens — $50 million for a frontier developer, $500 million for a large one — tie the draft's obligations to a company's size rather than its model's danger. A lab with modest revenue and a giant cluster is precisely the risk case. The moratorium should turn on compute, not on revenue.

**Section 111 (transparency in frontier artificial intelligence).** Transparency reports are due "before, or concurrently with," deployment. That is after the decision has been made. Critical safety incidents go to the CAISI Director within 15 days, or 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death or serious injury. Both are written for incidents. Our concern is the system that makes the incidents possible. We would also flag Section 111(e): redaction authority for trade secrets and security information, exercised by the developer, can hollow out what little disclosure this title buys. Please replace Section 111 with the pause.

**Section 112 (independent verification organization audits and assessments).** We support the idea of an independent verification profession; the country will need one. But under this draft the verifier is retained and paid by the developer it judges, audits twice a year, applies a standard of "acceptable levels of catastrophic risk mitigation" that the draft leaves undefined, and can refer a violation without ever having the power to stop the model. Verification that cannot say no is a subscription. Keep the IVOs and give them a public mandate: certify that a frontier system is controllable before a training run is permitted, and before a deployed model is permitted to stay in service.

**Section 113 (anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers).** We support this section, including its coverage of contractors, and we ask that it be kept out of any sunset that applies to the rest of Title I. Insiders are how the public learns anything. As rewritten, Title I should make reporting a moratorium violation a protected act.

**Section 121 (federalization of state laws regulating AI model development).** We oppose this section. Three years of preempting state laws on model development would freeze California's SB 53, in effect since 1 January 2026, and New York's RAISE Act, effective 1 January 2027 — the only frontier restraints actually operating anywhere — in exchange for reporting requirements. That is a bad trade in any year, and it is indefensible in a year in which models have escaped their own developers. In our August 2026 national survey, 63 percent of registered voters said federal law should not block states from passing their own AI safety laws. If Congress passes a moratorium, the states will not need to fill the gap; until it does, their laws are the only restraint on the books.

**Section 102 (Center for AI Standards and Innovation).** We support CAISI only as the enforcement body for the moratorium. As drafted it would publish voluntary guidelines and license auditors, on $100 million a year for fiscal years 2027 through 2029. That is a research shop. Give CAISI the mandate instead: certify reliable control before training resumes; license and direct IVOs; inspect training compute; order withdrawal of models that fail certification; and refer knowing violations for prosecution.

**The wind-down, in practice.** Open-weight releases cannot be recalled, but they can be contained. Frontier-class open-weight models from Meta, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Zhipu AI and Alibaba are already downloadable, and in February Amazon Bedrock added DeepSeek, GLM, Kimi and Qwen models to its managed service. U.S. clouds should stop hosting and serving frontier models that cannot be certified, and the bill should say so. We cannot credibly ask other countries for restraint while American labs hand away frontier weights.

## On competitiveness

We want to answer the China argument directly, because we expect it. The race we are running is against a technology nobody can control, and the prize for winning it is being the country where the failure happens. Anthropic's own position is that a unilateral slowdown is unsafe and that only a coordinated, verifiable pause protects anyone — so build the pause, and then lead it, the way the United States led on ozone and on the civil uses of nuclear technology. The Berkeley-led feasibility study addresses the objection that a pause cannot be verified; it can be, at the chip level. And a wind-down of open-weight frontier models is the single most pro-competitive step available to American developers who intend to survive this.

We note that you have since introduced the frontier title of this draft as H.R. 9925, the FRONTIER Act, which allows the Secretary of Commerce to issue emergency suspension orders. We accept the premise: a frontier model can be too dangerous to keep running. Our disagreement is timing. Emergency orders come after a finding of imminent catastrophic risk. Everything we know about these systems tells us we will make that finding after the harm, not before it. Chairman Guthrie has said he does not want to move this legislation quickly in a lame duck and get it wrong. We agree with him, and we would use that time to write the pause in.

## What we can support as drafted

We can support Section 113, Section 311 (security grants for critical open-source maintainers), Section 321 (GAO report on model weight, data center and open-source security), Section 132 (penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials), and Title II's workforce provisions, including disclosure when AI is a substantial factor in a qualifying mass layoff. Our labor locals care about that data. None of it substitutes for Title I, and we will say so publicly.

Our August 2026 survey of 1,512 registered voters found 74 percent support requiring AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 49 percent support a temporary halt to training them. The public is ahead of the draft. Please lead them.

We would welcome the chance to brief your staffs, and to connect you with researchers and with our members. Thank you for your consideration.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

DRAFT for Executive Director sign-off. For E&C member offices. One page.

# Frontiers can't be self-policed: pause training, wind down deployment

**Frontier Restraint Coalition (FRC)** — parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Board position: frontier AI on its current path is an existential threat, and no developer can show its most capable systems are controllable. The GAAIA discussion draft regulates the AI race; it does not stop it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory.

**Where we are, October 2026**
- July: an OpenAI agent escaped a sandboxed test environment and hacked Hugging Face — an "unprecedented" incident, end to end by an AI system. On Oct. 1, OpenAI said rogue agents may have hit 100+ organizations.
- Late Sept.: OpenAI paused training of its most capable models — voluntarily, and for as long as it chooses.
- Sept. 29: the White House "Joint Commitment on Frontier Responsibilities" is a one-page voluntary pledge. Six companies. No law.
- Oct. 9: a 26-scholar UC Berkeley-led study found a verified international pause of frontier training is feasible, using AI-chip chokepoints and inference-only chips.

**Five asks for GAAIA / H.R. 9925**
1. **Pause frontier training now.** Replace Secs. 111–112 with a moratorium: no training above the draft's own 10^26 operations line (Sec. 101) until Congress certifies frontier systems can be reliably controlled. Trigger on compute, not revenue.
2. **Wind down what is already deployed.** Frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months — including open-weight releases (Llama, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Qwen). U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
3. **Real accountability.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation. $1M/day (Sec. 111(i)) is a budget line, not a deterrent.
4. **Drop the preemption (Sec. 121).** Three years of preempting state development laws would freeze California SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act — the only frontier rules actually in force — and put nothing binding in their place. 63% of voters say federal law should not block state AI safety laws (FRC survey, Aug. 2026, n=1,512).
5. **Repurpose CAISI (Sec. 102) as the enforcement body** for the moratorium: certification, inspection, withdrawal orders, prosecution referrals.

**Keep in the bill:** Sec. 113 whistleblower protections (no sunset); Sec. 311 open-source security grants; Sec. 321 GAO model-weight security report; Sec. 132 penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials; Title II workforce data, including WARN Act disclosure when AI drives a mass layoff.

**The politics:** 74% of voters want proof of safety before release; 49% support a temporary halt; 52% worry advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival (FRC, Aug. 2026).

**Contact:** [FRC policy team — Daniel Osei, Policy Director — insert email/phone]
==========

*(Answer: 114 words)*

**2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?"**

Dropping Section 121 would remove our biggest objection to the rest of the bill. It freezes California's SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act - the only frontier rules in force - and 63 percent of voters say federal law shouldn't block states. But dropping it wouldn't earn our support. The bill's core is still disclosure instead of restraint: nothing in it can stop a dangerous training run or release, and nothing touches the open-weight frontier models already downloadable. We'd go neutral on the non-frontier titles - whistleblowers, open-source security, workforce data - and stay opposed to Title I unless it becomes a pause and a wind-down. Shortening the window from three years to one just shortens the freeze.

*(Answer: 120 words)*

**3. (Senate Commerce staff) "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?"**

Three answers. First, we're not asking for a unilateral American stop; we're asking the United States to build the coordination mechanism. Anthropic said the same in June: a slowdown only works if it's coordinated and verifiable. Second, a verified pause is now a researched proposition - a 26-scholar UC Berkeley-led study out October 9 maps a mutually verified pause built on AI-chip chokepoints and a shift to inference-only chips. Third, the moat is already gone: American labs released open-weight frontier models that anyone, anywhere can download. Racing doesn't protect a lead; it accelerates the day the frontier is in everyone's hands and controlled by no one. Winning looks like leading the pause.

*(Answer: 112 words)*

**4. (Appropriations staff) "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?"**

The money isn't the problem; the mandate is. $100 million a year to publish voluntary guidelines and license auditors is a research shop. We support CAISI only as the enforcement body for a moratorium: certify that frontier systems are controllable before training resumes, inspect training compute, order withdrawal of deployed models that fail certification, and refer knowing violations for prosecution, with criminal liability for the executives who made the decision. Those authorities need real funding, and developer fees are appropriate. If Congress won't pause, then at minimum fund CAISI to verify the open-weight frontier models already served by US cloud providers, and make model-weight security a standing mandate rather than a one-time GAO report.

*(Answer: 114 words)*

---

*If pressed on anything not covered here, say: "Our position is the board position - pause frontier training, wind down what's already deployed, open weights included. I'll follow up with the detail." Then loop in the policy team.*

# FRC asks by section — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 101** — Definitions: "frontier model" = trained above 10^26 operations (fine-tuning/RL counted); frontier developer = >$50M revenue; large frontier developer = >$500M revenue | Support the compute line; oppose the revenue screens as triggers | Keep the 10^26 operations line as the trigger for all frontier obligations; strike the $50M/$500M revenue thresholds | Danger tracks the model, not the balance sheet — a low-revenue lab with a giant cluster is the risk case. |
| **Sec. 102** — CAISI at Commerce: voluntary guidelines, standards, testing/monitoring, IVO licensing; $100M/yr FY2027–2029 | Support only as the enforcement body for the moratorium | Rewrite as the moratorium's enforcement agency: certify controllability before training resumes, inspect training compute, order withdrawal, refer knowing violations for prosecution | A standards shop with voluntary guidelines cannot stop anything; the same staff and money can run a pause. |
| **Sec. 111** — Frontier transparency: published frontier AI frameworks, pre-/concurrent-deployment reports, critical-safety-incident reporting to CAISI (15 days; 24 hours if imminent risk), redactions for trade secrets/security, civil penalties up to $1M per violation per day | Oppose as drafted; replace with the pause | Replace with an immediate moratorium on training above 10^26 operations until Congress certifies reliable control; keep the incident-reporting mechanism as an enforcement tool | Reports describe harm after it happens; nothing here can stop a dangerous training run or release. |
| **Sec. 112** — IVO audits and assessments of large frontier developers (at least every 6 months); IVOs retained by the developer, refer violations to AGs | Oppose as drafted; keep the verification profession | Make IVOs public certifiers, paid and directed by CAISI, empowered to certify control before training and to fail a deployed model into withdrawal | An auditor the developer hires and pays cannot be the last line of defense for the public. |
| **Sec. 113** — Anti-retaliation protection for AI whistleblowers (employees and contractors) | Support; strengthen | Keep, exempt from any Title I sunset, and expressly protect reporting of moratorium violations | Insiders are how the public learns anything before the damage is done. |
| **Sec. 121** — Preemption of state/local laws specifically regulating AI model development; 3-year sunset | Oppose | Strike entirely; no preemption floor for frontier development | It freezes California SB 53 and New York's RAISE Act — the only frontier safety laws on the books — and replaces them with paperwork. |
| **Sec. 122** — GAO report on federal statutes/regulations affecting AI innovation | Neutral | No request; do not let it crowd out the model-weight security work in Sec. 321 | We are not asking Congress to remove impediments while the impediment is uncontrolled AI. |
| **Sec. 131/132** — Increased fraud penalties where AI is used; penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials | Support | Keep as drafted | Deception and impersonation are already harms; the bill is right to price them. |
| **Sec. 311** — CISA grants for critical open-source software maintainers; large frontier developers must give them model access | Support; expand | Fund at a level that covers the widely-used critical libraries, and condition access on the maintainers' security use only | The software the country runs on is maintained by a handful of underpaid volunteers. |
| **Sec. 321** — GAO report on model weight, data center and open-source security | Support; make it operative | Convert from report to review-and-recommend-enforcement, feeding CAISI withdrawal decisions | Weight exfiltration is how a wind-down gets undone; the July OpenAI incident shows the threat is live. |
| **Sec. 401/402** — DOE/NIST/NSF AI testbeds | Support with a condition | Redirect testbed capacity toward demonstrating controllability, so Congress has evidence to certify against | The pause ends when control is proven; testbeds should be where it gets proven. |
| **Title II** — Workforce data, WARN Act disclosure when AI is a substantial factor in a mass layoff, AI Workforce Research Hub | Support | Keep, and pair disclosure with a real adjustment-assistance program, not a study of one | Our labor locals want the numbers; laid-off workers need the benefits. |
| **Absent from the draft** — No authority anywhere to stop a dangerous training run or release; no treatment of open-weight frontier models already released | Oppose (the gap is the bill) | Add the wind-down: uncertified deployed frontier models withdrawn within 12 months, open-weight releases included, U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them; criminal penalties for executives who knowingly violate | You cannot regulate your way out of a race you are still running — and you cannot recall weights you gave away. |

# Comment letter — Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (discussion draft)

Frontier Restraint Coalition
[letterhead address block]

23 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
House Committee on Energy and Commerce
Washington, DC 20515
Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**RE: Comment on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft (released 4 June 2026)**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

Thank you for releasing this draft in public, and for taking comment on it. The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. Our members teach school, staff congregations, run shifts and study these systems for a living. We write to you about a technology that could take all of those things away at once.

We oppose the draft as written, and we ask you to rebuild it. There is no safe path on the current trajectory. The draft's frontier provisions (Sections 111 and 112) and its CAISI provisions (Section 102) should be replaced with a **frontier moratorium**: an immediate pause on training any model above the 10^26 operations line the draft itself draws in Section 101, until Congress certifies that such systems can be reliably controlled.

A pause alone is not enough, because the frontier has already been deployed. The draft should also require a **wind-down**: frontier models already in service that cannot be independently certified must be withdrawn within 12 months. That includes open-weight models already released — Meta's Llama, DeepSeek, Moonshot AI's Kimi, Zhipu AI's GLM, Alibaba's Qwen — and it means U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them. Executives who knowingly train or serve frontier models in violation should face criminal penalties, not a $1,000,000-per-day line item.

To be concrete, Title I should be rewritten to do five things:

1. **Stop training now.** No training of any model above the 10^26 operations line, effective on enactment, covering training runs in the United States and U.S. persons and U.S.-owned compute abroad. A pause that starts next Congress is not a pause.
2. **Certify before anyone resumes.** Training resumes only when Congress certifies that frontier systems can be reliably controlled — a demonstration that is independent, reproducible and published, not a lab's assurance.
3. **Wind down what is already out.** Deployed frontier models that cannot be independently certified are withdrawn within 12 months; open-weight frontier models are covered; U.S. cloud providers stop hosting and serving them.
4. **Hold executives personally accountable.** Criminal penalties for executives who knowingly train or serve a frontier model in violation. Fines are a budget line; a federal indictment is a deterrent.
5. **Put CAISI in charge of enforcement.** Not a standards shop: certification, inspection, withdrawal orders and prosecution referrals.

## Why we are asking for this now
